title: Identification and Estimation of Treatment Effects with a Regression-Discontinuity Design
research_question: Under what conditions can the average causal effect of a binary treatment on an outcome of interest be identified and consistently estimated when the probability of receiving the treatment changes sharply at a known threshold of an underlying assignment variable? The paper asks how weak the assumptions can be made—allowing for heterogeneous effects and self-selection on anticipated gains—while still recovering a meaningful average treatment parameter for the population near the threshold.
data_description: This is a methodological note that does not analyze a specific dataset. The framework is developed for a generic cross-section of units indexed by i, each characterized by a binary treatment indicator x_i ∈ {0,1}, a scalar outcome y_i, and a continuous assignment (forcing) variable z_i whose density is positive in a neighborhood of a known cutoff z_0. Potential outcomes (y_{1i}, y_{0i}) and individual-specific treatment effects β_i are allowed to be heterogeneous. The authors reference several empirical applications that fit this data structure, including Thistlethwaite and Campbell's (1960) study of scholarships and career aspirations using test-score thresholds, Van der Klaauw's (1997) analysis of financial aid and college enrollment using GPA/SAT-based aid rules, Angrist and Lavy's (1999) class-size and test-score data based on Maimonides' rule, and Black's (1999) housing prices near school attendance boundaries.
institutional_context: The motivating settings are situations in which administrative rules, program eligibility criteria, or geographic boundaries generate a known, sharp change in the probability of treatment as a function of an observable score or location. Examples cited include merit scholarships awarded only when a test score exceeds a cutoff; college financial aid packages that depend on GPA and SAT score brackets; class-size caps in Israeli schools that force the opening of an additional classroom once enrollment exceeds a threshold (Maimonides' rule); and school-quality differences across geographic attendance zones that capitalize into housing prices. In each case, units just above and just below the rule-induced threshold are plausibly similar in unobserved characteristics, yet face very different probabilities of receiving the program or treatment, creating a natural comparison for evaluating policies such as marginal changes in eligibility cutoffs.
